questions.stem: What is one astronomical unit (AU)?
options: The distance from the Sun to the nearest star
The mean distance between Earth and the Sun
The distance light travels in one year
The mean distance between Earth and the Moon
questions.explanation: One astronomical unit is the mean Earth-Sun distance, about 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, and is convenient for distances within the solar system. The distance light travels in a year is the light year, which is about 63 000 AU.

questions.stem: Which statement about the light year is correct?
options: It is a unit of time, equal to one year measured in a moving frame
It is a unit of distance, the distance from Earth to the nearest other star
It is a unit of distance, the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year
It is a unit of time, the time light takes to cross the whole solar system
questions.explanation: Despite the word year, a light year is a distance: about 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ × 3.16 × 10⁷ s ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. The nearest star beyond the Sun is a little over 4 light years away, so the two are not the same.

questions.stem: How is the parsec defined?
options: The distance from the Sun to the centre of the Milky Way
The distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of one arcsecond
The distance at which 1 light year subtends an angle of one degree
The distance light travels in a vacuum in one hundred years
questions.explanation: A star one parsec away shows a parallax angle of one arcsecond (1/3600 of a degree) when viewed from opposite sides of Earth's orbit, because the radius of the orbit, 1 AU, subtends that angle there. One parsec is about 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, or 3.26 light years.

questions.stem: A star is 4.2 light years from Earth. What is this distance in metres?
questions.explanation: One light year is 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m, so 4.2 ly = 4.2 × 9.46 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 4.0 × 10¹⁶ m. The 6.3 × 10¹¹ m answer uses astronomical units instead of light years, and 1.3 × 10¹⁷ m uses parsecs.

questions.stem: A star cluster is 10 parsecs away. How far is this in light years?
options: 3.1 ly
10 ly
33 ly
questions.explanation: One parsec is about 3.26 light years, so 10 pc ≈ 32.6 ≈ 33 ly. Dividing by 3.26 instead of multiplying gives 3.1 ly, and 2.1 × 10⁶ comes from converting to astronomical units instead.

questions.stem: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Neptune, about 30 AU from the Sun?
options: About 4.2 hours
About 8.3 minutes
About 30 minutes
About 4.2 years
questions.explanation: Light takes about 1.496 × 10¹¹/(3.00 × 10⁸) ≈ 500 s, or 8.3 minutes, to travel 1 AU. For 30 AU it takes 30 × 500 s ≈ 1.5 × 10⁴ s, about 4.2 hours. The 8.3 minutes is the time to reach Earth.

questions.stem: About how many astronomical units are there in one light year?
questions.explanation: Divide the light year by the astronomical unit: 9.46 × 10¹⁵/(1.496 × 10¹¹) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁴ AU. The 2.1 × 10⁵ value is the number of AU in a parsec, and 3.3 is the number of light years in a parsec.

questions.stem: A star shows a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds. How far away is it?
options: 4.0 pc
4.0 ly
questions.explanation: From the definition of the parsec, the distance in parsecs is 1 divided by the parallax angle in arcseconds: 1/0.25 = 4.0 pc. A smaller parallax means a more distant star. The answer is in parsecs, not light years; 4.0 pc is about 13 ly.

questions.stem: Which unit would be most convenient for stating the distance between two neighbouring galaxies?
options: The megaparsec
The astronomical unit
The kilometre
The light second
questions.explanation: Neighbouring galaxies are typically millions of light years apart, so megaparsecs (10⁶ pc) give manageable numbers. Astronomical units suit distances within the solar system, and kilometres or light seconds would give numbers far too large to be convenient.

questions.stem: What does the Big Bang theory describe?
options: A universe that has always existed with the same density as today
The formation of the solar system from a collapsing cloud of gas
The universe expanding and cooling from an extremely hot, dense early state
An explosion of matter outward from a point into existing empty space
questions.explanation: The Big Bang theory says the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since. It was not an explosion into pre-existing space: space itself expands, so there is no centre. A universe of constant density is the rival steady state idea.

questions.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, where in the universe did the Big Bang happen?
options: Everywhere, since all of space was contained in the early dense state
At the centre of the Milky Way, which is why galaxies recede from us
At a point near the edge of the universe, from which galaxies spread
At a point that can be found by tracing galaxies' motions backwards
questions.explanation: In the Big Bang model space itself expands, so every point was part of the early hot, dense state and there is no centre. Every observer, in any galaxy, sees distant galaxies receding. Our seeing galaxies recede does not put us at the centre.

questions.stem: As the early universe expanded, it cooled. Which sequence of events does the Big Bang theory describe?
options: Protons and neutrons formed, then light nuclei, then neutral atoms, then stars
Neutral atoms formed, then stars, then light nuclei, then protons and neutrons
Stars formed, then protons and neutrons, then light nuclei, then neutral atoms
Light nuclei formed, then protons and neutrons, then stars, then neutral atoms
questions.explanation: As the universe cooled, quarks combined into protons and neutrons, which fused into light nuclei such as helium within the first few minutes. Neutral atoms formed hundreds of thousands of years later, and the first stars and galaxies hundreds of millions of years after that. Each stage needed a lower temperature than the one before.

questions.stem: Why could neutral atoms only form once the universe had cooled to a few thousand kelvin?
options: Above that, collisions and radiation had enough energy to knock electrons off atoms
Above that, the strong nuclear force could not hold protons and neutrons together
Above that, electrons had not yet formed from the decay of protons and neutrons
Above that, gravity was too weak to pull electrons into orbit around nuclei
questions.explanation: At higher temperatures typical photon and particle energies exceeded the ionisation energies of hydrogen and helium, so any atom that formed was quickly ionised. Once the universe cooled enough, electrons could stay bound to nuclei. Nuclei themselves had formed much earlier, and electrons are bound by the electric force, not gravity.

questions.stem: What is the cosmic background radiation?
options: Radio waves sent out from Earth that have been reflected back by distant gas
Microwave radiation arriving almost evenly from all directions in the sky
Gamma radiation given off by the radioactive decay of rocks in Earth's crust
Visible light from the combined glow of all the stars in the Milky Way
questions.explanation: The cosmic background radiation is faint microwave radiation that fills the sky almost uniformly. It matches the spectrum of a black body at about 2.7 K. It is not starlight or terrestrial radioactivity, and it comes from every direction, not just from the Milky Way.

questions.stem: How does the Big Bang theory explain the cosmic background radiation?
options: It is radiation produced continuously as new matter is created throughout empty space
It is radiation from the Sun, scattered back to Earth by the solar wind
It is radiation from the hot early universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths by expansion
It is radiation from the first stars, absorbed and then re-emitted by cold dust in our galaxy
questions.explanation: When the universe became transparent, the radiation then filling it was characteristic of a body at a few thousand kelvin. As space expanded, the wavelengths stretched, and the radiation now matches a black body at about 2.7 K, in the microwave region. Continuous creation of matter is the steady state idea, which predicted no such radiation.

questions.stem: The cosmic background radiation has a spectrum matching a black body at about 2.7 K. Why does this support the Big Bang theory?
options: A temperature of 2.7 K shows that the universe is no longer expanding
A black body spectrum shows that the radiation comes from stars like the Sun
A temperature that low shows that the radiation was produced very recently
A cooled remnant of radiation from a hot, dense early universe was predicted
questions.explanation: The Big Bang model predicted that radiation from the hot early universe would still fill space, cooled by expansion to a few kelvin, with a near-perfect black body spectrum. Its discovery in 1965 matched that prediction. The low temperature is the result of expansion, not evidence that it has stopped.

questions.stem: The cosmic background radiation is extremely uniform across the sky, with tiny variations of about one part in 100 000. What do these tiny variations indicate?
options: Errors in the measuring instruments, which have been corrected in later surveys
Radiation from nearby galaxies that adds to the background in some directions
Regions of space that have not yet been reached by the expanding universe
Slight differences in density in the early universe, from which galaxies later grew
questions.explanation: The tiny variations record slightly denser and less dense regions in the early universe. Gravity later pulled matter into the denser regions, forming galaxies and clusters. Without them the universe would have stayed smooth. They are confirmed by several independent satellite missions, so they are not instrument errors.

questions.stem: The cosmic background radiation was first released when the universe became transparent. Why did this happen when neutral atoms formed?
options: The first stars switched on and their light pushed away the gas
Free electrons, which scatter light strongly, were captured into atoms
Neutral atoms emit microwaves, which pass easily through space
Protons and neutrons combined into nuclei, which do not absorb light
questions.explanation: Before atoms formed, the universe was filled with free electrons that constantly scattered photons, so light could not travel far. When electrons were captured into neutral atoms, photons could travel freely, and that light is what we now see as the background radiation. Nuclei had formed long before, and stars came much later.

questions.stem: By mass, roughly what proportion of the ordinary matter in the universe is hydrogen and helium?
options: About equal parts hydrogen, helium and heavier elements
About three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium
About one-quarter hydrogen and three-quarters helium
About half hydrogen and half heavier elements
questions.explanation: Observations of stars and gas clouds show about 75% hydrogen and about 25% helium by mass, with only small amounts of heavier elements. The Big Bang model predicts these proportions from the fusion that occurred in the first few minutes.

questions.stem: Why is the observed abundance of helium in the universe evidence for the Big Bang?
options: Helium is the product of radioactive decay, which was faster in the early universe
Helium can only form at very low temperatures, like those of space today
Stars could not have made so much helium, but the hot, dense early universe could
Helium is made only in supernovae, and these were common in the early universe
questions.explanation: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium, but not fast enough over the age of the universe to produce the 25% observed everywhere. The Big Bang model predicts that fusion in the first few minutes, while the universe was hot and dense enough, made about this much. The prediction and the observation agree closely.

questions.stem: Which statement about the origin of the light elements is consistent with the Big Bang theory?
options: All elements heavier than hydrogen formed only when the first stars exploded
Hydrogen and most helium formed in the early universe; heavier elements formed later in stars
All elements, including iron and gold, formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang
Hydrogen formed inside the first stars, while helium formed in the early universe
questions.explanation: Big Bang nucleosynthesis produced hydrogen, most of the helium and traces of other light nuclei such as deuterium and lithium. The universe cooled too quickly to make heavier elements, which formed later inside stars and during the destruction of stars.

questions.stem: The dark lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy appear at longer wavelengths than in a laboratory. What does this tell us?
options: The galaxy is hotter than the Sun
The galaxy contains heavier elements
The galaxy is receding from us
The galaxy is approaching us
questions.explanation: A shift of spectral lines to longer wavelengths is a red shift, which shows the galaxy is moving away from us. A shift to shorter wavelengths, a blue shift, would mean it is approaching. The pattern of lines identifies the elements; the shift tells us about motion.

questions.stem: What relationship did Hubble find between the distances of galaxies and their red shifts?
options: All galaxies have the same red shift, whatever their distance from us
Nearby galaxies are red shifted while distant ones are blue shifted
More distant galaxies have larger red shifts, so they recede faster
More distant galaxies have smaller red shifts, so they recede more slowly
questions.explanation: Hubble found that a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance, v = H₀d, so more distant galaxies show larger red shifts. This is what is expected if space itself is expanding uniformly. A few nearby galaxies are blue shifted, but because of local gravitational motion, not distance.

questions.stem: How does the Big Bang theory explain the red shift of light from distant galaxies?
options: Space expands while the light travels, stretching its wavelength
The light loses energy by collisions with dust, lowering its frequency
Distant galaxies are made of elements whose lines are all at longer wavelengths
Gravity of the Milky Way pulls on the light, increasing its frequency
questions.explanation: In an expanding universe the wavelength of light is stretched along with space as it travels, so light from more distant galaxies, which has travelled longer, is more red shifted. Elements emit the same wavelengths everywhere, which is why the shift can be measured. Falling into the Milky Way's gravity would blue shift light slightly, not red shift it.

questions.stem: Taking H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, at what speed does Hubble's law predict a galaxy 50 Mpc away is receding?
options: 0.71 km s⁻¹
1.2 × 10² km s⁻¹
3.5 × 10³ km s⁻¹
1.4 km s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Hubble's law gives v = H₀d = 70 × 50 = 3.5 × 10³ km s⁻¹. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 1.4 km s⁻¹ or 0.71 km s⁻¹. Units of km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ mean the speed rises by 70 km s⁻¹ for every megaparsec of distance.

questions.stem: Taking H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, how far away is a galaxy receding at 7.0 × 10³ km s⁻¹?
options: 4.9 × 10⁵ Mpc
10 Mpc
1.0 × 10² Mpc
questions.explanation: Rearranging Hubble's law, d = v/H₀ = 7.0 × 10³/70 = 1.0 × 10² Mpc. Multiplying gives 4.9 × 10⁵ Mpc, and H₀/v gives 1.0 × 10⁻² Mpc.

questions.stem: On a graph of recession velocity (km s⁻¹) against distance (Mpc) for many galaxies, the points lie close to a straight line through the origin. What does the gradient of the line give?
options: The age of the universe
The speed of light in km s⁻¹
The distance to the edge of the universe
The Hubble constant, H₀
questions.explanation: Hubble's law, v = H₀d, has the form y = mx with velocity on the vertical axis and distance on the horizontal, so the gradient is H₀ in km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. The age of the universe can be estimated from 1/H₀, the inverse of the gradient, not the gradient itself.

questions.stem: If galaxies have always receded at their present speeds, the time since they were together is d/v = 1/H₀. Taking H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km, what age does this give?
options: About 1.4 billion years
About 140 billion years
About 14 billion years
About 4.4 billion years
questions.explanation: 1/H₀ = 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km/(70 km s⁻¹) ≈ 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s. Dividing by about 3.16 × 10⁷ s per year gives about 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years, or 14 billion years, close to the accepted age of about 13.8 billion years. The 4.4 figure is the time in seconds, 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s, misread as years, and the other two are slips in the power of ten.

questions.stem: A larger value of the Hubble constant is measured. If the expansion rate has been constant, what does this imply about the age of the universe?
options: It is older, because galaxies have had longer to spread apart
It is unchanged, because the age does not depend on H₀
It is older, because faster expansion needs more time to begin
It is younger, because the age is estimated from 1/H₀
questions.explanation: A larger H₀ means galaxies at a given distance recede faster, so they would have taken less time to reach their present separations. The estimated age, 1/H₀, is therefore smaller. This is why disagreements over the value of H₀ matter for the age of the universe.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that space itself is expanding, rather than galaxies simply flying apart from a central point?
options: Observers in every galaxy would see all distant galaxies receding according to Hubble's law
The Andromeda galaxy is approaching the Milky Way and shows a blue shift in its light
Galaxies in one region of the sky show red shifts, while those opposite show blue shifts
The most distant galaxies show red shifts that are the same as those of nearby galaxies
questions.explanation: In a uniformly expanding space, every observer sees the same pattern: galaxies receding with speeds proportional to distance, with no special centre. Andromeda's blue shift is a local gravitational effect within our group of galaxies, and the other two patterns are not what is observed.

questions.stem: The Andromeda galaxy shows a blue shift. What does this show?
options: It is much hotter than other galaxies near the Milky Way
It contains no hydrogen, so its spectral lines are missing
It is moving towards the Milky Way, drawn by gravity
It is moving away from the Milky Way, faster than light
questions.explanation: A blue shift means the galaxy is approaching. Andromeda and the Milky Way are close enough that their mutual gravity outweighs the expansion of space between them. Hubble's law describes the overall trend for distant galaxies, not the local motions of nearby ones.

questions.stem: A galaxy is 100 Mpc from Earth, and 1 pc = 3.26 ly. Roughly how long ago did the light now reaching us leave it?
options: About 3.3 billion years ago
About 330 million years ago
About 100 million years ago
About 33 million years ago
questions.explanation: 100 Mpc = 100 × 10⁶ × 3.26 ly ≈ 3.3 × 10⁸ ly, and light takes one year to travel each light year, so it left about 330 million years ago. Distant galaxies are therefore seen as they were long ago. Treating megaparsecs as millions of light years gives 100 million years.

questions.stem: Express a Hubble constant of 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ in SI units, using 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m.
questions.explanation: Convert the speed to metres: 70 km s⁻¹ = 7.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. Then H₀ = 7.0 × 10⁴/(3.09 × 10²²) ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Leaving the speed in km s⁻¹ gives 2.3 × 10⁻²¹, and 4.4 × 10¹⁷ is 1/H₀, which has units of seconds, not s⁻¹.

questions.stem: Space is expanding, yet the Milky Way and the solar system are not getting larger. Why not?
options: The light from nearby objects is too bright for any expansion to be detected
Gravity binds them together far more strongly than the expansion pulls them apart
Expansion only began recently, after the Milky Way and solar system had formed
Expansion only occurs in empty space beyond the edge of the observable universe
questions.explanation: On the scale of planets, stars and galaxies, gravity holds matter together and the effect of the expansion is overwhelmed, so these systems do not grow. Expansion shows up between distant galaxies and clusters that are not gravitationally bound. It has been happening throughout the history of the universe.

questions.stem: Which list gives evidence that supports the Big Bang theory?
options: Galaxies' red shifts, the Moon's craters and the age of Earth's rocks
Light-element abundance, the solar wind and the colours of the nearby bright stars
Cosmic background radiation, light-element abundance and galaxies' red shifts
Cosmic background radiation, sunspot cycles and the orbits of the outer planets
questions.explanation: The main evidence is the cosmic background radiation, the observed abundances of hydrogen, helium and other light elements, and the red shifts of galaxies following Hubble's law, which show expansion. Sunspots, planetary orbits and the Moon's craters are solar system features that tell us nothing about the origin of the universe.

questions.stem: Before 1965, some scientists favoured a steady state theory in which new matter forms as the universe expands, keeping its density constant. Which discovery counted most strongly against it?
options: The spectra of stars, showing that they contain hydrogen and helium
The cosmic background radiation, a cooled remnant of a hot, dense early universe
The red shift of distant galaxies, showing that the universe is expanding
The parallax of nearby stars, showing that they are light years away
questions.explanation: The steady state theory also accepted an expanding universe, so red shifts did not distinguish the two. It had no hot, dense past and so no natural way to produce a uniform black body background. The discovery of the background radiation in 1965 therefore strongly favoured the Big Bang.
